title: Fellowship vs Internship: What's the Difference, and Which One Fits You?
summary: Fellowship vs internship: compare stipends and wages, funding, length and selectivity, plus the main fellowship types and where each goes on a resume.
body_markdown:
The fellowship vs internship question confuses people because the two words sound like the same thing. They aren't. An internship is a short stretch inside an employer's team. A fellowship is funding that an organization gives you to study, research or build something specific, and it's one of the 11 formats in our guide to the[types of internships compared](https://www.extern.com/post/what-is-an-internship-types) .


We sit down with a lot of students one-on-one, and we hear this mix-up two ways. Some skip every fellowship listing because they assume fellowships are only for PhDs. Others treat the word as a fancier label for an internship, then get a surprise when the money arrives as a stipend.


So this guide compares the two using the terms that funders like the National Science Foundation publish and the IRS rules on how the money is taxed. Then it shows where each one belongs on your resume.


## TL;DR


• A fellowship is a funded, selective award for study, research or a defined project, usually paid as a stipend. An internship is a short, supervised work experience with an employer, usually one to three months, paid hourly or unpaid.


• The money works differently. The NSF Graduate Research Fellowship pays a $37,000 annual stipend for three years, while interns at the bachelor's level average $23.35 an hour, according to NACE.


• Fellowships exist at every stage: summer research programs for undergraduates, awards lasting several years for graduate students, and post-graduate fellowships such as Fulbright.


• A stipend isn't a wage. The IRS treats fellowship money as tax-free only when a degree candidate spends it on tuition, required fees, books and supplies.


• On a resume, a fellowship with real work behind it goes under Experience, same as an internship.


[Externships](https://www.extern.com/post/what-is-an-externship) are short, remote professional experience programs where you work on real projects with real companies. If you'd like to test a field before you write a proposal or an application, the[HP Tech Ventures Deal Sourcing & Startup Analysis Externship](https://www.extern.com/externships/hp-tech-ventures-deal-sourcing-startup-analysis-oct-2026) , the[TruBridge Healthcare Data Analytics Externship](https://www.extern.com/externships/trubridge-healthcare-data-analytics-externship-oct-2026) and the[Lean Startup Co. Corporate Strategy Externship](https://www.extern.com/externships/corporate-strategy-externship-mentored-by-the-eric-ries-oct-2026) are open now.[Explore all Externships](https://www.extern.com/externships) .

## What Is the Difference Between a Fellowship and an Internship?


A fellowship pays you to pursue study, research or a defined project, and a funder selects you for it. An internship puts you inside an employer's team for a short time so you can try the work. One is built around your project. The other is built around theirs.


### What Is a Fellowship?


A **fellowship** is a funded, selective award that supports a person's study, research or work on a defined project for a set period. The[IRS](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc421) describes a fellowship grant as money paid to help an individual pursue study or research. The money follows the person and the purpose, not a job opening.


In practice, the award is tied to something concrete, like a thesis or a year of teaching abroad.


### What Is an Internship?


An **internship** is a short, supervised work experience with an employer that lets a student or recent graduate try out a field. It can be paid or unpaid, and the employer decides what you work on. The[U.S. Department of Labor](https://www.apprenticeship.gov/help/what-difference-between-apprenticeship-and-internship) says internships usually last one to three months. It also says it has no official definition of the term.


So the contrast isn't prestige. It's who sets the agenda and who pays.


### Fellowship vs Internship at a Glance


Line them up and the two differ on nearly every practical point.


Feature Fellowship Internship


**Main purpose** Fund your study, research or a defined project Let you try a field inside an employer's team


**Typical length** One summer to several years, set by the award Usually 1 to 3 months


**Money** Usually a stipend. Example: $37,000 a year on the NSF Graduate Research Fellowship Hourly wage or unpaid. Bachelor's-level interns average $23.35 an hour (NACE, 2026)


**Who funds it** A government agency, foundation or university, and sometimes a company The employer


**Employment status** Often not an employee of the funder Usually a temporary employee. An unpaid intern may not legally be an employee


**How you apply** Written application, often with a proposal or statement, a transcript and reference letters Resume, sometimes a cover letter, then interviews


**Who it suits** People with a defined question, field or mission Students still comparing fields, or aiming at one employer


**Who confirms it in a background check** Usually the sponsoring organization The employer


**Resume section** Experience, with the award also listed under Honors if you like Experience


---


## What Kinds of Fellowships Are There?


Fellowships show up at three stages: during college, during graduate study and after a degree. The word means something different at each one, so check the stage first.


### Undergraduate Fellowships and Research Programs


Undergraduate fellowships are usually short, funded research or project experiences, and most happen in summer. They're the closest cousin of a research internship. What separates them is where the money comes from: a grant or an endowment, not a company's payroll.


The National Science Foundation's[Research Experiences for Undergraduates](https://www.nsf.gov/funding/initiatives/reu/students) program is a good reference point. According to NSF, a typical site hosts around 10 students who work on related research projects, mostly over the summer. They're paid stipends. Many sites also help with housing, meals and travel. You apply directly to each site, and it's open to U.S. citizens, nationals and permanent residents.


### Graduate and Research Fellowships


Graduate fellowships fund the years you spend earning a research degree. They're the largest awards, and the terms are public.


Two federal examples show the scale:


• **NSF Graduate Research Fellowship Program.**[NSF](https://www.nsf.gov/funding/opportunities/grfp-nsf-graduate-research-fellowship-program) provides three years of support within a five-year fellowship period for students in research-based master's and doctoral programs in STEM. Each year of support carries a $37,000 stipend, plus a $16,000 allowance that goes to the university in place of tuition and mandatory fees. The current solicitation estimates 1,500 awards.


• **NIH Kirschstein-NRSA fellowships.** For fiscal year 2026,[NIH](https://grants.nih.gov/grants/guide/notice-files/NOT-OD-26-044.html) set the predoctoral stipend at $29,364 a year. Postdoctoral stipends start at $63,480 and rise to $77,076 with experience.


Nobody would mistake either one for a summer job.


### Post-Graduate and Professional Fellowships


Post-graduate fellowships fund a defined period of study, research, teaching or service after a degree. The[Fulbright U.S. Student Program](https://us.fulbrightonline.org/about/fulbright-us-student-program) is a well-known example. It's open to graduating college seniors, graduate students and young professionals, and it works in partnership with more than 140 countries. Fulbright grants include[a stipend based on the cost of living in the host country](https://us.fulbrightonline.org/about/award-benefits) , and the length depends on the award.


The word has two other uses worth knowing. In medicine, a fellowship is education in a subspecialty, according to the[ACGME](https://www.acgme.org/about/overview/) . And some employers put the fellowship label on short programs for people early in their careers; if you're on the payroll earning an hourly wage, treat it as an internship.


---


## Do Fellowships Pay, and How Is a Stipend Different From a Wage?


Most fellowships pay, but usually as a stipend. Internships that pay do it with wages. The words sound alike, yet the difference touches your taxes, your benefits and what you owe in return.


### How a Fellowship Stipend Works


A **stipend** is a fixed amount meant to cover your living costs while you do the work the award supports. It isn't tied to hours. NIH says so directly in a[2023 policy notice](https://grants.nih.gov/grants/guide/notice-files/NOT-OD-23-111.html) : its stipends are a "subsistence allowance," and they aren't provided as a condition of employment.


The practical result: a fellow on a stipend often isn't an employee of the funder, so there may be no timesheet, no overtime and no employer benefits unless the host institution adds them.


Taxes work differently too. Under[IRS Topic No. 421](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc421) , fellowship money is tax-free only if you're a degree candidate and you spend it on tuition, required fees, books, supplies and equipment for your courses. Amounts used for room, board or travel are taxable. So are payments for teaching, research or other services the award requires.


We said a stipend isn't a wage.


But that doesn't make it tax-free, and it's the part people most often get wrong. Your award letter and your school's financial aid office can tell you how yours gets reported.


### How Intern Pay Works


A paid intern is an employee earning a wage. According to NACE's[2026 Guide to Compensation for Interns & Co-ops](https://naceweb.org/talent-acquisition/internships/hourly-wage-for-interns-climbs-but-is-down-over-last-10-years-in-real-terms) , interns at the bachelor's level averaged $23.35 an hour.


But can an internship pay nothing? At a for-profit employer, only when the intern is the main beneficiary. The Department of Labor's[Fact Sheet #71](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fact-sheets/71-flsa-internships) sets out a "primary beneficiary test" with seven factors, and if it shows you're working as an employee, you're owed minimum wage and overtime.


Our guide on[whether interns get paid](https://www.extern.com/post/do-you-get-paid-in-an-internship-guide) has the detail.


---


## How Are Fellowships Funded, and How Selective Are They?


Fellowships are funded by an organization with a mission, and internships by an employer with work to get done. That one difference explains most of the others, including how you get chosen.


### Who Pays for Each One


Fellowship money usually comes from a third party: a federal agency such as NSF or NIH, a government exchange program, a private foundation or a university endowment. The funder wants a result that fits its mission, so you answer for the plan you proposed.


An internship is paid for out of the employer's own budget, and that holds for government internships and nonprofit internships too. The organization is investing in a possible future hire, so you answer to a manager and that team's priorities.


Is one arrangement better? No.


But it shapes your days more than the title does.


### Selectivity and What the Application Asks For


Fellowships select on your plan and your potential. Internships select on fit for a role. Both can be hard to get, and we haven't found a trustworthy acceptance rate that covers all fellowships, so we won't quote one.


A typical fellowship application runs like this:


1. **Find the award and read the eligibility rules.** Citizenship, degree stage and field limits vary, so check them before you write a word.


2. **Write the proposal or personal statement.** That's where most of the time goes, so start it before anything else.


3. **Line up reference letters early.** NSF says REU applications often ask for a transcript, a statement of interest and reference letters, and here's[how to ask a professor for a letter of recommendation](https://www.extern.com/post/how-to-ask-a-professor-for-a-letter-of-recommendation) .


4. **Plan for the lead time.** Deadlines often fall many months before the start date.


An internship application is lighter: a resume, sometimes a cover letter, then interviews. Volume and timing are the hard part. Our list of the[best websites to find internships](https://www.extern.com/post/best-websites-to-find-internships) shows where postings appear.


---


## Which One Is Right for You?


Choose the fellowship if you have a specific question or mission and you're comfortable working without much supervision. Choose the internship if you're still testing fields or you want a particular employer to know you.


### When a Fellowship Fits and When an Internship Fits


**A fellowship fits when:**


• **You have a defined question or project.** Funders back plans, so a clear one does most of the work in your application.


• **You're headed toward research, policy or graduate school.** A competitive award carries weight there.


**The trade-offs of a fellowship:**


• **The application is long.** Proposals and reference letters take weeks, with no guarantee at the end.


• **You may not be an employee.** That can mean no employer benefits and a tax bill you have to plan for.


**An internship fits when:**


• **You're still comparing fields.** A summer inside a team tells you fast whether you'd want the job.


• **You want a route into one employer.** Many employers hire from their intern class.


**The trade-offs of an internship:**


• **Pay isn't guaranteed.** Some placements are unpaid or pay only a small stipend, which rules them out if you need the income.


• **The work is assigned.** You'll support the team's priorities, which may have little to do with your own interests.


Already graduated? Our guide to[internships after college](https://www.extern.com/post/internship-after-college-guide) covers which programs take graduates.


### What If You're Between the Two?


Plenty of students land between these two: no research proposal yet, and no room for a full-time summer internship.


Other formats fill that space. A co-op builds full-time work terms into a degree. We compare it in[co-op vs internship](https://www.extern.com/post/co-op-vs-internship-guide) . An apprenticeship is a paid job with structured training that lasts years, and[apprenticeship vs internship](https://www.extern.com/post/apprenticeship-vs-internship-guide) explains when that makes sense. An Externship is a short, remote professional experience built around a company project and guided by an extern manager. Most run 8 weeks. The range is 4 to 11 weeks, at 5 to 10 hours a week, and our[externship vs internship](https://www.extern.com/post/externship-vs-internship-guide) comparison walks through the differences.


At Extern, we've seen students use a short project to find out whether they like independent work before they commit to a long fellowship application. In our post-program survey (1,001 responses through June 2026), students rated the experience 8.7 out of 10 on average. If operations and people analytics interest you, the[Amazon Fulfillment Center Operational Strategy & People Analytics Externship](https://www.extern.com/externships/amazon-fulfillment-center-operational-strategy-people-analytics-oct-2026) is one example.


Your situation matters more than the label on the program.


Your situation Best fit Why


**You have a research question and a faculty mentor** Research fellowship Funding to pursue your own project


**You are an undergraduate who is curious about research** Summer undergraduate research program A stipend, a small cohort and a project led by faculty


**You are comparing two or three industries** Internship Short, supervised and inside a working team


**You are finishing a degree and want a funded period of study, research or teaching abroad** Post-graduate fellowship Awards such as Fulbright are open to graduating seniors and young professionals


**You want one specific employer to hire you** Internship An internship is how many employers pick future hires


**You need something remote that fits around classes** Externship 4 to 11 weeks at 5 to 10 hours a week, built around a project

## How Do You List a Fellowship or Internship on a Resume?


Both usually go under Experience. The reason is more useful than the rule, because it sorts the rest of your resume too.


### The Background Check Test


**Where does an experience go on a resume?** Ask one question: can it be confirmed in an employment background check? If an organization will verify your dates and your role, the experience belongs under Experience. If all you have is a certificate of completion, it belongs under Projects or Certifications.


Fellowships are usually confirmed by the sponsoring organization, meaning the agency, foundation or university that made the award. Internships are confirmed by the employer. Externships on Extern support employment background checks.


Here's how each entry looks:


• **Fellowship:** list it under Experience with the sponsor and your title, for example "Research Fellow, Sponsoring Organization, September 2025 to June 2026." Name the funder if it's different from the place where you worked.


• **Internship:** list it under Experience with the employer, your title and the dates, for example "Policy Intern, Employer Name, June to August 2026," with bullets on what you delivered.


One exception. An award that only paid tuition, with no work attached, reads better under Honors or Awards.


Our article on[resume claims and background checks](https://www.extern.com/post/lie-on-resume-background-check) explains what employers verify.


### How Recruiters Read Each One


We've spent years on the recruitment process outsourcing side, watching how employers screen candidates at the start of their careers. Here's how the two lines tend to land.


A fellowship reads as selection. A recruiter sees that an outside organization chose you from a pool, then trusted you to work independently. In research, policy and graduate admissions, that counts for a lot.


An internship reads as exposure, plus a signal that an employer picked you. Recruiters look at where it was, how long it lasted and, above all, what you produced.


Yet fellowships have a weak spot. Outside the fields that use them, plenty of recruiters won't recognize the name of your award. Add one line that says who funded it and how you were selected.


Building a first resume? Start with our guide to a[resume with no experience](https://www.extern.com/post/resume-with-no-experience) , or see[how to list an Externship on your resume](https://www.extern.com/post/externship-on-resume-boosts-credibility) .


Both applications reward an early start, and a finished project helps in either one. You can[browse open Externships](https://www.extern.com/externships) .

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Is a fellowship better than an internship?


Neither is better across the board. A fellowship is the stronger choice if you have a defined research question, field or mission and can work on your own. An internship fits better if you're still comparing industries or hope a specific employer will hire you after graduation.


### Do fellowships pay more than internships?


It depends on the award. Many fellowships pay a fixed stipend instead of an hourly wage. NSF's Graduate Research Fellowship pays $37,000 a year, while interns at the bachelor's level averaged $23.35 an hour in NACE's 2026 compensation guide. Some internships are unpaid.


### Can undergraduates get a fellowship?


Yes. Many funded programs are built for undergraduates, especially in research. The National Science Foundation's REU sites take groups of around 10 students, mostly in summer, and pay stipends. Your campus fellowships office lists college awards, and Fulbright accepts applications from graduating seniors.


### Does a fellowship count as work experience?


Usually, yes. If your fellowship involved research, teaching or a placement, list it under Experience with the sponsoring organization, your title and the dates. The sponsor can usually confirm it if an employer checks. A fellowship that only paid tuition belongs under Honors or Awards.


### Is a fellowship stipend taxable?


Often, at least in part. According to IRS Topic 421, fellowship money is tax-free only if you're a degree candidate and it pays for tuition, required fees, books and supplies. Money for room, board or travel is taxable, and so are payments for services the award requires.
